source: សៀវភៅស្ដីពីដំណាំដំឡូងមី (Book on Cassava), Part 2 - production, processing, market development and export improvement, UNDP-supported capacity-building programme for cassava, Phnom Penh, Cambodia, March 2015
text:
Cassava (Manihot esculenta Crantz) is a tuber crop with a long history of cultivation in Cambodia, historically grown mainly by poorer farming households in small home-garden plots as a supplementary food and livestock-feed crop. In more recent years, the area planted to cassava has expanded substantially because the crop requires comparatively less labor and fewer inputs than many alternatives, while offering good income potential and strong market demand, both domestically and for export, particularly to Thailand and Vietnam. Existing farmland previously used for other crops, as well as newly cleared land, has increasingly been converted to cassava production.

The source notes that continuous cassava monocropping, especially on the same land year after year, depletes soil nutrients (particularly where organic matter or fertilizer is not replenished) and can lead to erosion on sloped land, raising sustainability concerns that the document frames as a reason for combining production growth with better agricultural practices, quality management, and market-development support.

The source cites research by Aye et al. (dated around 2014) on efforts to improve cassava-farming hygiene, disease/pest management, and product quality and safety in order to meet requirements of export destination markets, particularly China. Three categories of capacity-building/training support are described: (1) Training of Trainers (ToT) for extension staff and lead farmers on disease diagnosis and cassava production/processing issues; (2) direct farmer training on recognizing and managing disease symptoms; and (3) training for buyers/collectors and traders on quality standards required for exported cassava and on requirements set by destination countries.
caveat: This is a new source for the cassava knowledge base (processed as cassava Source K), distinct from the agronomy-focused Source G training course (Batch 46). Its focus is market development, processing, quality standards, and export procedure rather than field agronomy. The precise historical area-growth figures mentioned narratively in the source (e.g., an early reference to roughly 30,000 hectares expanding to over 400,000 hectares over about a decade) are treated as approximate narrative context; see the companion topic file 'production_area_statistics_2010_2013' for the more precisely transcribed statistical table covering 2010-2013.
